utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to these data, you are a farmer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And before that, you worked in the police?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you worked in the Zrze police station?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked at the police station at Rahovec, and Xerxe is a substation of Rahovec police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you worked at Zrze, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in Rahovec, for the police station in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you retired as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as of which date did you receive a pension as a retired police officer?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of 1988, in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, at a certain point in time in the police, because your -- of your exceptional merits, you were awarded and received a carbine as a gift as an exemplary worker of the police force?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I don't know where you got that information. I bought it with my own money because I was a hunter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not receive it as a gift for your merits from the police. That information is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no need to repeat it. He said it wasn't a gift.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, you describe the killing of five Serb policemen on the 22nd of April in your village of Meja. Is it true that this happened on the 21st of April?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true -- no, on the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just checking because, according to information I have, it was not the 22nd but the 21st. But after all, that is not so important for your testimony. Do you know that among the killed policemen, one was an Albanian policeman, Arifaj Naser; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have been Albanian. I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in addition to those policemen, a policeman called Milutin Doncic was seriously wounded and that his right leg had to be amputated at the hospital in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And before this act of terrorism in your village and the immediate vicinity, in the course of 1998 and the first months of 1999, were there terrorist acts committed by the KLA against civilians, the police, the army? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of the KLA committing any acts against civilians. 1998 -- in 1998 there were acts. From the 2nd of August on, there wasn't any KLA there, around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who, then, committed those acts if it was not the KLA? Who is it that opened fire on civilians, the police, and the military?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that the whole area was surrounded with tanks, police, army from all sides, and that's when the incident took place. I don't know who did it, I just know that the whole place was surrounded by tanks and police, the whole village in Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And while it was surrounded by the police and the army, they killed those six policemen. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, how far is the village of Batusa from your village?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Batusha's about 20 kilometres from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you hear of the expulsion of the entire Albanian population of that village, consisting of 80 households? Did you hear that they had been expelled by members of the KLA in 1998 who had come from Albania? Are you aware of that event?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. It's not true that the KLA expelled the population. The KLA defended the population as far as it was able.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, how far is the village of Smolica from your village, a village that you mention in your statement on page 1, Smolica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Smolica is near -- is about ten kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Had you heard that in this village in 1998 there was the main base of the KLA terrorists for Djakovica and also the centre for collecting and distributing weapons brought in from Albania?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the KLA in this village dug out several kilometres of trenches from which they opened fire on the police?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And had you heard of the killing of the soldier Dragan Ignjatovic, Marko Matic, Dejan Ristic, Dusan Tasic who were brutally murdered by the KLA in Smolica in 1998? Are you aware of that event?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I haven't heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And next to this village, you also mention in your statement the village of Nec. Do you know that the KLA terrorists, in 1998, forced the Albanian Catholic and Muslim population to leave the village and that a half went to Junik and the other half to Cardak?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, because all the population, all the families were defending their own houses. They were all together. They all left together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And had you heard that at the time KLA members set fire, in Smolica, all haystacks and the complete harvest?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you ask that again? I didn't quite understand what you were getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Had you heard that at the time, in the village of Smolica, the KLA torched all the haystacks and the complete harvest?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't imagine that happening, that a people would burn its own food sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they did not burn their own food sources. It is the KLA who burnt it in the village of Smolica, burned the harvest of the farmers there.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, because the people needed to eat. It can't possibly be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that it is even less probable, following your own logic, for them to kill civilians, including Albanians, and they still did so and in quite large numbers, as you know. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I don't agree with you at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that you disagree with me. You were born in the village of Ramiz. Do you know that in that village there was local security elected by the inhabitants of the village themselves with the support of the state which provided them with weapons to protect themselves from these bandits? Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And had you heard of an incident on the 26th of February in 1999 when in that very village of Ramiz where you were born, the KLA wounded three members of the local security force, all Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you heard of the killing of an Albanian called Fadil Tolaj by the KLA on the 11th of March 1999 in the village of Meja, where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never heard that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you an eyewitness or do you know anything at all about -- since you left the village of Meja, according to your own statement, on the 22nd of April, 1999, so do you know anything about the bombing of a column of Albanians in the vicinity of your village on the 14th of April when more than 80 men, women, and children of Albanian ethnicity were killed and dozens wounded? Do you know anything about that event?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was two kilometres away from my home. The planes flew very low that day, and everyone said that it wasn't NATO but it was Serb planes. That was our view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pnishi. Even NATO has admitted to that bombing, so we have a saying, "You don't have to be a greater Catholic than the Pope." Did you go to visit the site yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not personally. I didn't dare go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You weren't interested in seeing what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. I didn't dare. I was interested, but it was difficult to go there. The -- the son of my brother went and -- went there and helped bury the victims, but I didn't go personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In connection with the killing of the policeman that you mention at the beginning of your statement, you stated that you don't know who was behind this act but that afterwards, what you call the incident, many of your neighbours sought shelter in your own house. Is that right, Mr. Pnishi?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I was at home when there was shooting, when there was bombing two kilometers away, and a few minutes later, the army came from Gjakove and they were shooting, shooting everywhere, in the air. We heard that people were killed. Milutin Prascevic and four colleagues of his were killed. There was shooting down the road independent of whether people were involved or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you -- I'm asking you in connection with the people who sought shelter in your own home. Did any of those who sought shelter in your home take part in the attack against the police?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Their house was near the main road, ten or 15 kilometres away, and they didn't even dare go out of their house. They stayed in a big basement room. We were at my brother's place, Gjelosh. At 9.15 or 9.30, there was a shot that came in through the window. It was firing with a sniper gun which came through the window. Fortunately, it didn't hit my brother but hit the wall opposite, broke the glass. And at 4.00, 4.30, there was shooting again at my brother's place, and the window was broken in. So that's the day we left our house and went to a village farther away, Jahoc, which is farther away from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, amongst those who were sheltered in your home, how many were armed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was armed. That I can tell you sincerely. No one had an arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you counted tanks on the 31st of July, 1998, near the border, and you mentioned the alleged attack on the villages of Nec, Smolica and Dobros. Do you call an attack the conflict between the police and the army with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What else can you call it? There we are, sitting in our own villages, and the Serbian police and army came and attacked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But please explain. Why do you call the conflict between the police and the army and the KLA as an attack on the village?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an attack on the village because the KLA in Kosova never went to Serbia to attack villages there. They were around their own homes, defending their own property. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware of the fact that that territory, that is, Kosovo, is also Serbia and that there's no question of going from Kosovo to Serbia because Kosovo is Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can deal with that. It's a rhetorical point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were a policeman. If you come across a group of terrorists shooting at the police, at the army, at citizens, civilians, Serbs, Albanians, and so on, do you consider that to be their right because they're living on that territory? Because after all, bandits operate in the territory in which they live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is all argument. The witness is simply describing what happened to him. He can't do more than that. As for the character of the conflict and what happened, that's something we're going to have to rule about in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you can rule that today is Monday, but do you see that every conflict by these witnesses of yours, conflict between the police and terrorist groups, is qualified as an attack on a village, as if some women were milking cows and the wild Serbian police come to kill them. These are highly organised groups of terrorists, as you can see, who were killing, slaughtering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can make your arguments in due course. All that you can argue to us in due course. But right now, you're engaged in cross-examining this witness, and the recent questions have all been matters of argument with him. Now, if you've got some further questions, some relevant questions for him, you should ask them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the questions are relevant. And especially this one is relevant, because in answer to a question why he describes a conflict with the KLA as an attack on the village, his explanation was that it is because they live there. So such an explanation is very useful for us to have to be able to understand what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your time -- your time is limited, as you know, so you need to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a Serbian family Prentic living in your village?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the 6th of May, 1998, did members of the KLA fire at the house of that family from a hand-held -- from a mortar and from automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the -- there was fighting, but I swear to this Court that every Albanian -- that no Albanian would fire like that, and only the Serbian police would fire in that way in order to use it as a pretext to imprison and arrest us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that this was the police of the Republic of Serbia which attacked that Serbian house in your village with a mortar and from automatic weapons? Is that what you're claiming, Mr. Pnishi?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no attack with a mortar, only with an automatic rifle, with 12 bullets from an automatic rifle that were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But did the Serbian police attack the house of this Prentic? Is that what you're claiming, that it was the Serbian police that used automatic rifles to attack the house of your neighbour Prentic, the person of -- your co-citizen from Meja? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can swear to God and to the Court that on that night, the police were drinking until half past ten that night. And when they came out, outside in the street between my house and his, when I came out, they fired at the -- at the roof of the house, not at the window. They aimed very well. And those two policemen went -- and they went to Korenica, and I swear -- I can swear that I saw them with my own two eyes as clear as day. And on the same -- on the next morning, I heard that they were firing the day before, and I'd seen everything that had happened from the balcony that night, and I saw it and I related it the next day. And then the police went and found the cartridges. We knew this very well. But we ourselves didn't dare go out to investigate what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So please tell me now, when did this happen? Because you happened to know this specifically, and I mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was more than one occasion when the house of the Serb family was shot up? Did it happen more than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only on that night. Only that night, no other occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There you are, Mr. Milosevic. That's your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I'm asking the witness when did this happen, because he describes this event so precisely, and he says that he remembers everything, so I'm asking him when did that happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've given him the date, the 6th of May, 1998. You've given it to him. It was the only occasion the house was shot up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he seems to have forgotten in the meantime. Perhaps he could have said it if he knew it. But very well. I need to hurry up because you will deny me the opportunity of questioning him within ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And page 2 of your statement, you describe how four soldiers with rifles pointed pushed Kole Duzhmani in the direction of your house. Were these people soldiers or police officers? You said there were two members of the MUP and two Russian soldiers. Can you tell me what these Russian soldiers are? Who are they?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that morning, as I mentioned in my statement, with my wife, my son Mark came, we did our jobs, and the Serbian army and police had been previously prepared during the night, and started firing in the air. At that moment, the APC arrived at my house and started firing above, in the hills above Meja. Kole Duzhmani from Korenica had been on a bike and had went to Jahoc and was setting off to his own house, and they stopped him and they mistreated and tortured him at my own front door. And -- and they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, I'm going to interrupt you. You were asked about the Russians specifically. Now, can you tell us about them, what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They -- as soon as I opened the door, there were four, and they said, "Open -- open the door." And I knew that they were not Serbs. I opened the door, and there were two masked Serbian policemen --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, there is no need to describe the event that you already described. I asked you: How is it that you know that they were soldiers, and what were Russians doing in the Serbian military and the police?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can tell very easy from the way they speak whether they're Serbian or Russian. In fact, about 30, 40 per cent of the Serbian language resembles the Russian one, but there's difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet many Russians in your life?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have met Russians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you speak Russian?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that the Russians didn't know how to read the information that was written in the alphabet, in the Roman script. The fact that they're Russian doesn't necessarily mean that they cannot read the Latin script.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's a matter of comment. Can you -- yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just as a point of fairness here, the statement actually states, and I'm looking at page 5 of the English, the fourth full paragraph, the witness states that the Russians could not read the Albanian language. There's no reference to the Roman script there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I suspect the reference to the Roman script is a reference to Albanian. Yes. The point is -- just one moment. Let's try and clarify this. The point that's being made is how did you know they were Russians, and you say you could tell from the language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Help us about the script. What was the point about the script? Did you see them reading something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard them talking, and they were talking to me, and I knew from that that they weren't Serbs. And they beat me and wanted to throw me in the well. And they were talking Russian among themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that you heard shots from the direction of your brother's house and that 19 days after you heard those shots, you found this Kole Duzhmani, you found his body, and based on that, the fact that you found him 19 days later, you claim that he was killed by those soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, because they left me -- they left me in the yard, and they put Kole Duzhmani in my brother's house. And my brother's wife had 12-year-old daughter on her hand, and they wanted to slit my son's throat, and then my brother-in-law got hold of my son by the arm and took him on the road to Albania, and they entered -- and on that very same day, they found Kole Duzhmani, and they had 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Exactly that what you have said confirms that you are saying here what others have told you, but that doesn't confirm anything. It doesn't say who killed Kole Duzhmani or when they killed him. Isn't that right, Mr. Pnishi?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment they took him from my house, they shot him and they burnt all the rooms in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know who it was that fired when you found that man dead 19 days after that day when you met those people that you claim are Russians?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, as soon as I left the door of my house, I ran to the window and looked at my brother's courtyard. When my sister-in-law went outside and set off for Albania, then they went in my brother's house and they did the execution there. We found the body on the nineteenth day because we couldn't go there any earlier. We dared not go there any earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I was only asking you how is it that you were able to conclude 19 days later when he was killed, who killed him, and so on. But there is a more interesting claim in your statement, and also based on what you said yesterday. You said that -- let's see first. Do you know how many members of the KLA were killed in the fighting with the army and the police in those days that -- during the period that you are testifying about? Do you know how many of them were killed in fighting with the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know. You claim here that about -- that a policeman killed about 11 of them. Then you claim that later in June you found traces of burnt bodies and that you estimate that 74 bodies were burned. Yesterday you spoke about how 412 bodies, dead bodies, were loaded onto a truck and a tractor, which you don't mention in your statement at all. So could you please explain to me this progression from the 11 who were probably killed in fighting, if there had been any fighting, so there were 11 dead, to these 74 that you claim that you found burned, and then to these 412 that you mentioned yesterday but which you do not mention in your statement, that were transported. Please tell me what this is all about, Mr. Pnishi. What is this story that you are telling here?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please make up the sentence in shorter parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I had to ask a more detailed question, a longer question, because I will be interrupted soon. But let's put it this way: Did you see with your own eyes that someone killed an Albanian at any time? Is that what you're saying that you saw, these 11? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is that before I left my house that morning, the convoy that was coming in the direction of Korenica-Gjakove, the commander of the police from Ponoshec, his name was Dragutin Guta, he came out on a vehicle type Cadet, black colour, and parked it across the asphalt road so nobody could proceed on that road. Every person, every young man, every youth was supposed to leave the tractors lying on the asphalt road. And the convoy would proceed only with elderly persons, and those who would remain behind would be executed. When the police withdrew in the direction of the school, in the direction of the checkpoint which was the main checkpoint, I went to the house and went to the third floor to see what was going on outside. I saw four policemen, Serb policemen, who brought seven persons, and they stopped them near the wall or the bridge, and one of the policemen shot them there at the bridge. And I was there on the third floor, and I could see this very well. And I know this policeman very well as well. Who he is, I've mentioned it already in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you claim that you saw the killing of seven persons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that you saw this personally?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my own eyes, I swear. Because as the crow flies, it was not more than 60 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these seven were killed by that one person that you say you know. So you know the person who killed these seven people.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are an ex-police officer. Did you go to report this man? Did you go to the police station where you used to work to report this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I went to report this, I wouldn't have been here today. I wouldn't have been alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Even though this is not true, let's leave that. So this seven that you say that you saw that personally, but where do these 412 persons come from? How did these seven people in some strange way become 412 people? Did you see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To be fair to the witness, he never said that he saw 412 people. What he said was it was something he'd been told about, something he had heard about, that was all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. If this is the place to hear what -- who told what to whom, then we could hear many stories like that. Some incredible things are being allowed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see even a single person out of those 412? Did you see even a single body out of those 412 bodies that you were told about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw those seven when they came and placed them together with the other group. Some others who were also going by tractor, the truck returned from the direction of Korenica in the direction of the Meja cemetery, and the tractor was waiting for the truck at that position. Then when they -- they together proceeded in the direction of the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're coming back to these seven. Did you see anybody else, any other bodies other than those seven that you claim you saw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very important, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You'll get an answer to this question. Mr. Pnishi, the question is: Did you see any other bodies other than the seven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to those seven that I mentioned, the first day after our liberation, at the Meja cemetery there were about ten bodies. Six other graves were opened in our cemetery, and there were three other bodies also decomposed. And then the foreigners would come, and then they would see the bodies and they would come to a conclusion that there were bodies there. You know, he was your worker, the one who with his sons packed the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now you are talking about bodies that you saw after the war. You saw them after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what -- that is what his statement says, in fact, that he'd seen bodies after the war. Now, we must bring this to an end. You've had more than your time. Mr. Kay, have you any questions? No, Mr. Milosevic, we cannot go on arguing in this way. You have your 45 minutes. You've had it and five minutes more. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, did I ask any irrelevant questions? Did I spend time asking irrelevant questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You spent plenty of time on the first part of his statement, which was more or less relevant. And then if you do that, it means that you don't have time - and this happens all the time with the witnesses - you don't have time for the second part. Now, what you should do is organise your cross-examination in such a way that you concentrate on the important matter. But you don't do that and this is what happens; you get brought to a close. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, you've testified in response to questioning by the accused that you saw Kole Duzhmani being led by the two Russian soldiers and the two police officers into your brother's house. You testified also that you then heard some shots and some 19 days later found the dead body of Mr. Duzhmani, with gunshot wounds, in your brother's house. If you can remember, could you please tell us approximately how much time passed between the time you saw Mr. Duzhmani being led into your brother's house by these four and the time that you heard the gunshots?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It could be a whole -- a total of five minutes, not any more. They went in, they took him in, and then they tried to slit my son's throat. Then they went into my brother's house, then I heard the shots, then the rooms were burning. It was about five minutes altogether, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, because I'm ignorant to the Russian language, if you could help me with this: In your statement, page 5 of the English version, you said relating to the Russian soldiers, I quote: "After the Russian soldier answered, the person on the other end of the radio ordered, 'Unisti ga.' That means 'Destroy him.'" I'm not sure my pronunciation is good. "Unisti ga" is Russian?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true that I understood what you are saying. And from outside the wall there, they were talking through their radios. The Russian took the radio outside and asked, "Is Gjelosh Kola there?" He was Serb, because if -- he was a Russian, because if he was a Serb, he would have understand what is "Kola." Then he said, "Unisti ga," which means "destroy him as soon as possible," and then they took Kole, they took him to my brother's house and they executed him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, before the next witness comes in, there is one matter which I want to deal with. It concerns the evidence of K13, a witness whose statement was admitted, as I recollect, under the Rule 92 bis. It has not yet been, as far as I can see, exhibited. Perhaps you would attend to that and make sure that is done. It's important it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour. Sometimes we go through the work and we don't actually file the documents. So we'll certainly attend to that, perhaps during the next break, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it? I didn't get a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on. According to this new schedule, I see that the next witness is Baqaj Gani. This doesn't bother me in the least, the fact that he has now been brought out of order, but yesterday I remarked about the inclusion in 92 bis, which you did not agree to but about this witness, I think -- of course it's your right not to take into account any of my remarks and put everything -- treat everything as 92 bis, but with this witness, I would like to say that this witness will testify about a wide number of questions which relate to arms smuggling from Albania, cooperation with the Albanian army, and a series of other things. And he is not suitable as a 92 witness. I cannot question this witness in only 45 minutes. So I suggest that before we -- before you reject my request that he not be treated as a 92 bis witness, I ask you to read his statement in order to see that it is not possible to cross-examine him in 45 minutes in view of the number of issues that he will testify about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider the application and consider how long it's appropriate for you to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness can take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm going to ask, again for the benefit of anyone wanting the spelling of Mr. Baqaj's name, that the spelling of his name be put on the ELMO. And I bring that to the Court's attention because I have misspelled the name in the summary. I put B-A-C-A-J and it's B-A-Q-A-J. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Baqaj, do I understand correctly, sir, that you are a 36-year-old Kosovar Albanian?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And I ask that you keep your voice up so that everyone can hear you, sir. Sir, in your original statement, your birth date is recorded as being the 1st of April, 1966. You have subsequently advised that your birth date is in fact the 1st of August, 1966; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And it's right, sir, that you're married, you have two children, and that you served your military service in the Yugoslav army between 1987 and 1988; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You joined the KLA in June of 1998. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it -- did you give your original statement to members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 27th and 28th of March of the year 2000? Did you provide a statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And subsequently, on the 9th of March of this year, 2002, did you have an opportunity to review that statement and make a correction such as the spelling of your name and the -- your date of birth and then tell the officer of the -- presiding officer of this Tribunal that the contents of your statement were true and accurate to the best of your information and belief?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Subject to any -- Your Honour, I would tender the statement that has been -- I believe it's here available now -- as our next exhibit. While that is happening, I just remind Your Honours that this witness will be talking about Dubrava Prison which, as in the other witnesses you've heard, is located in the Kosovo atlas at page 5, J12. It's about six or seven kilometres east of Istok. If I may read while that's happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. On the 2nd of September, 1998, the witness was first arrested by Yugoslav soldiers at the Albanian-Montenegrin border, was taken to an army barracks, and then transferred to another barracks where he was interrogated by two men in civilian clothes. In his statement, he outlines that he was beaten and tortured between 10.00 p.m. that evening and 6.00 the next morning. Then, under military escort, he was taken to Nis, to Pristina, and then to Gjakove. From here, on the 5th of September, he was taken to the Peja police station where he was further interrogated and physically mistreated. He knew, and therefore names, two of his interrogators in his statement. Unable to take any more beatings, he admitted membership in the KLA. He was then detained in Peja prison.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read more slowly, Mr. Ryneveld. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I've been admonished to read more slowly. The witness was transferred, with another around 20 other prisoners, to Dubrava Prison in Istok on the 21st of December, 1998. He was housed in cellblock C1 and identifies his cellmates. Also in C1 block were ten Serbian prisoners who wore prison uniforms. They were kept segregated from the Kosovar Albanian prisoners. And C1, Your Honours will recall, was the C block labelled the isolation block in Exhibit 289 that you've heard other witnesses testify about. The witness states that he was taken to Peja court on the 4th of February where he was found guilty of arms smuggling, guarding his village, and being a member of the KLA. He was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment and then returned to Dubrava Prison. On the 21st of February, 1999, he was transferred to C2 block, where most of the convicted prisoners were housed. His evidence will include the fact that from around the beginning of March 1999 to the end of April, 1999, additional prisoners were transferred from other prisons in Serbia to Dubrava and that some civilians from Gjakove town were also brought to and detained in Dubrava. Hence, at the end of April of 1999, the prison population, he would estimate, was nearly a thousand inmates. Well, the witness tells you in his statement that on the 19th of May, 1999, NATO bombed the prison, killing three prisoners in C1 block. After this incident, the prisoners were allowed to remain out in the compound. On the 21st of May, NATO bombs, in a more prolonged bombing attack, killed approximately 19 more prisoners. The Serb guards ordered the witness and the other prisoners to take the wounded to the sports field and to cover the dead where they lay with blankets. He spent the night of the 21st of May down a large drain, along with other prisoners. On the morning of the 22nd of May, 1999, guards ordered the prisoners to line up on the sports field, telling them that they were being transferred to Nis prison in Serbia. He tells you in his statement that there were around 10 lines of prisoners. He was in the front line with friends approximately 30 metres from the watchtower facing him. He saw three people dressed in guard uniforms and wearing black masks with eye holes standing in the tower. Two had automatic weapons and one had a bazooka-type weapon. To his right he saw a figure outside the perimeter wall in green camouflage uniform, saw that individual stick a heavy machine-gun through a hole in the wall. That hole, he says, had been caused by NATO bombing. On this person's right sleeve he saw the word "Milicija." The guards and milicija began shooting at the prisoners. He heard the sound of firing all around. He was terrified and lay face down on the ground. He heard the screaming from the wounded around him and obviously general panic amongst the prisoners. He describes that the shooting lasted, in his opinion, for around half an hour, after which he crawled about 50 metres before running to the kitchen basement where he sought refuge with about 300 to 400 other prisoners. Throughout the day, snipers fired from the watchtowers. He spent that night in the kitchen basement. The next morning, between 5.00 and 6.00 a.m., he saw about 20 masked men wearing uniforms and an unmasked man in a guard uniform surround the kitchen. Grenades were thrown inside and a voice shouted in Serbian, "You have five minutes to come out or we'll kill you all." Those in the basement surrendered and were marched to the gymnasium where they were ordered to sit on the floor. While in the gymnasium, the witness heard a masked man outside say, "We will kill them all inside and people will think that NATO killed them." He could hear shooting continuing outside and the sounds of exploding grenades. Two hours later, a masked man came into the gym with five cartons of cigarettes and told the prisoners that the commander, Miki, had sent them the cigarettes and they would no longer be harmed. After this announcement, they had freedom of movement inside the prison. The witness indicates that he went with others to the sports field where they counted the bodies of 160 dead prisoners. Dead prisoners were also found in the drains. Together -- altogether, the witness will say that, including the 23 prisoners killed by NATO, according to his count, 190 Dubrava prisoners had been killed. On the 24th of May, all surviving prisoners were transferred by bus to Lipjan prison. The wounded followed in trucks. They were told by guards not to talk about or discuss what had happened in Dubrava and that if asked, they should say NATO killed all the prisoners. Well, very briefly, then: On the 10th of June, he was transferred to Sremska Mitrovica prison where he served the remainder of his sentence and was released on the 6th of March, 2000. Now, Your Honours, you have already seen Exhibit 289, but I would like to just ask the usher to show the -- the attachment that you have in the 92 bis package of the Dubrava Prison which shows the watchtower, and I just want to ask a couple of questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Baqaj, you can see it on the screen, but I'm going to ask you actually to use something and point on the document itself so it will show on the screen. I'm particularly interested, sir, in the sports field and the watchtower and that incident that you described in your statement. Can you briefly indicate on this document, this map that you have initialed, could you briefly show us where the prisoners were and where the shooting came from and where you went.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: The prisoners were in the gymnasium there, all in lines, and the person -- people who shot -- were shooting were up in the watchtower and over there on the right side where there was a hole in the wall which had been made -- caused by NATO. And I was about there, out in the field somewhere, in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: In a row. We were in rows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that the gymnasium or sports field?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's my first question of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you said, "We were in the gymnasium." Did you mean gymnasium or did you mean the sports field? Where the men were lined up.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No, I meant the sports field.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And pointing to that -- just show us again this area that is immediately below the word "watchtower" where we have a sort of a triangle formed by the word "watchtower," that area right in front of that, for the record, is that the sports field to which you are referring?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: In the corner there, at the top, that's the watchtower. And the sports field is right under it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: These lines, these ten lines of men, how many persons would you estimate were lined up facing in those ten -- facing the watchtower in those ten lines?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: There were about 800, 850, I would say, prisoners facing the watchtower there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: One final question about that, sir -- from me, at least. The hole in the wall that you pointed to, just to the right if we're looking at the perimeter wall, you said there was a hole caused by NATO bombing. How large was that hole, approximately?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: The hole on the right wing was about 70 centimetres high and about 50 centimetres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would that hole be large enough for a person to go through?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: It was difficult for a person to go through it because it wasn't quite a big hole for a person to crawl through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: At least, not a person of my size, I take it. Would you -- you're somewhat slender; would you have been able to go through that hole?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes, but I guess with efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, was that hole large enough, for example, for a truck to drive through? I'm sorry, I didn't get a response.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No. A tractor could not pass through that hole. The hole was not that big.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Finally, sir, of the people that were killed in the sports field as a result of the shooting incident, do you recall any of the names of those people killed that day on the sports field by the activities of the individuals you described on the 22nd of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I remember certain persons who were near me. I had several bodies that were around me, so I can remember those names of those bodies who were near me. Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Please state them.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: -- number the names, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Please, yes.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: There was a person from municipality of Decan, from the village of Istinic, whose name was Met Osmanaj. Besim Paqarizi was also close by. He was from Prizren. Naim from the village of Streoc, also from the municipality of Decani. Ramiz Memija from Albania, from Tropoje. Hamdija Demaj [phoen] from the village of Racaj. Fadil Beqiri from Racaj as well, and Izet Beqiraj from the municipality of Gjakove. These were the persons near my position, persons whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are my questions. Just one final thing: The photograph that I've asked the witness to refer to is part of the bis'ing package. Do you want it made a separate number or just leave it as part of the package?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, you said that you joined the KLA in June 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of your unit?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: There was -- we didn't have a commander at that time in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of your unit? I'm not talking about the village. You were part of a unit.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I was a member of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear you very well. What were you, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I was a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A member of the KLA, and that is why I'm asking. How many men did your unit number?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: All the village was -- were -- formed part of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question. How many men were in your unit?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: There are about 250 homes in the village. I said that all the men in the village were members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the unit numbered about 1.000 men? Maybe a little more, a little less?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: The whole village was in the unit with the exception of a few individuals who were loyal to the Serb state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what kind of weaponry did you have?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: We had an automatic -- automatic rifles. Correction: I had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you all have automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No, not all had automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did the others have, then?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: There weren't enough arms for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. When you started bringing weapons from Albania, were there sufficient weapons then?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No. There were just some people went to get arms for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, when did all of you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know when everyone had arms. I just know that I had an automatic weapon and that some individuals went to Albania to get arms for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were one of those persons who went to Albania to get weapons. That's right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I went with some friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And before we move on to that subject, that is, to your travels to Albania to get weapons, tell me, in how many battles did your unit take part involving the killing of policemen, officers -- army officers, and civilians? In how many battles, how many operations?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: There were no actions in my village undertaken by the KLA. I'm talking of the time when I was in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in any killing of a policeman, a soldier, or a civilian, and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I did not take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you fire from that rifle that you say that you and the others had?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't fire a single bullet during this war.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No, because I had my engagements with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Mr. Baqaj, let us now focus on your activity. You mentioned that you were arrested on the 2nd of September on the border between Albania and Yugoslavia on the Yugoslav side of the territory at Bozhaj and that you were arrested by the army.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You crossed the border illegally, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were you put up in Albania?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I was with my family in Durres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, in those days and on all other occasions while staying in Albania, you were collecting weapons, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And while staying in Albania, were you involved in the training of KLA members in camps in Albania?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No, because as I said, I had engagements with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Baqaj. In the statement that you made to our investigating authorities, which is attached to your statement to The Hague Prosecutors, you said that in April, on the 24th of April, 1998, a meeting was held in the village mosque. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us skip over that topic. Is it true that Ramush Haradinaj signed a certificate with which you went to Tropoje in Albania to take over some weapons there?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: With some friends that I went with in Albania, we didn't have any documents with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when you crossed into Albania, were you without documents? But did you have that document at any point in time at all?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you leave it?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I said we did not have any document with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You told the investigating authorities that in Tropoje officers of the Albanian army met you and that they took you in military trucks to the town of Bajram Curri. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: With my family, when I went there with my family, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what ranks did those officers hold?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the time has come for an adjournment. We'll consider your application for more time during the adjournment. Mr. Baqaj, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Could you remember, please, during this adjournment not to speak to anyone about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Would you be back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've considered the question of time. You can have an hour with this witness, which means that you have another 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't get an answer to my last questions. What ranks did the officers have, the ones who were waiting for you at the border?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I said I don't know what kind of ranks they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many soldiers from the Albanian army were there together with them?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see any soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you go to Albania for weapons?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I went once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: It was about the middle of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of you were there in the group then?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: When I went, there were about 15 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many weapons did you bring across on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: When I went, we all brought back one each.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You told the Yugoslav investigating authorities that -- you said that when you crossed the border to Albania, you met a column of Albanians, about 200 of them, who had 200 horses with them which were loaded with weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I didn't say that they were with weapons, but I said that they were with their womenfolk, going to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these people who were transporting weapons from Albania, were they Albanians from Kosovo or were they Albanians from Albania?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see them carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the people that you met, were they Albanians from Kosovo or were they Albanians from Albania who were crossing into Yugoslavia over the border?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I said I saw them -- I saw women, children, the elderly crossing the border going into Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that now, but in your statement to the Yugoslav investigative authorities, you said that you saw 200 horses loaded with weapons. Each horse was led by a guide, a person who was leading the horse. Is that so or isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, it occurs to me that Your Honours have not had the opportunity of seeing the document on which the witness is now being cross-examined. It was part of the disclosure package, and in order for this to make any sense to Your Honours, I wonder whether you should have a copy of it available to you. I only -- this has not been reviewed with the witness either. It was part of the disclosure package but not something led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let us have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I also wonder, since the witness has not seen this, there is a copy in B/C/S, might he be provided with it as well? The witness has not -- this has not been reviewed with the witness prior to his giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Provided this doesn't take up too much time, it can be done. I don't want to waste more time than is strictly necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I'm just trying to think of fairness to the witness and the fact that Mr. Milosevic appears to be choosing to spend time on this aspect rather than on the evidence that he's been led on and that's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The eighth line on page 3 is the passage that the accused is questioning on at the moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have the document now. I asked you already and you denied it, but in your statement, it says: "Two days before we went to the Republic of Albania on the 24th of April, 1998, the four mentioned persons organised a meeting in the village mosque which was attended by 50 villagers, among them my brother Baqaj Haki. It was decided at the meeting that we would leave for the Republic of Albania in two days and that anybody who applied could go. On the 26th of April, in the evening hours, in the village of Aljaj, 50 members of the DTG, the sabotage terrorist group, got together. Aljaj Bujar was appointed the leader of the group since he knew the road towards the Albania very well." And then you name all of those who crossed over. And before that, you say that this was at Haradinaj Ramush's initiative, the commander of the Main Staff, that it was on his initiative that this operation was carried out. You talk that on the return of the group from Albania, a headquarters was formed in the house of Ramadan Dukaj who was appointed commander of the staff while the others -- the other persons were also members of the staff. And their names were Bujar Aljaj and Shemsedin. Before that, you say that you remained for seven days in the KLA headquarters in the village of Busidoj [phoen] near Tropoje, and that these people were forced to buy the weapons with their own money, and so on. At one point, you say during -- "When we were crossing over the border, we met a caravan of about 200 horses loaded up with weapons and about 200 members of the DTG, of whom one-half were from the Drenica area and the rest from Junik. In addition to the others, Sadrija Gacaferi was in the column who told me that the weapons had been collected from the staff of the so-called government of the Republic of Kosovo in Tropoje." And then you say: "When we arrived at the entrance --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We need to see where you're reading from. Mr. Kay, can you assist us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has your -- this has the markings 00002948. I'm reading from the Serbian text. I'm reading from the first paragraph of that text, and it's 2950. That is the number on the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 3 in the English at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say: "When we arrived at the entrance to Tropoje, we were greeted by Albanian army officers who transported us in military lorries to the town of Bajram Curri where we were accommodated in private homes. My family and I were housed with Hasan Avdija for a month. After three days, I went to the Three Brothers Cafe in Bajram Curri and there I met Muhamet Nitaj from Drenovac who pointed --" I cannot read this -- "who pointed out Tahir Zemaj, a former JNA officer from the village of Streoc, Fadil Haradinaj from the village of Sllup, Decani municipality, a certain Aba born in Drenica, and their driver who had a beard and black glasses. He told me that they had recently arrived from Germany and were in the staff of the so-called government of the Republic of Kosovo in the village of Hodjaj near Tropoje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, Mr. Milosevic. This is cross-examination. The witness should have the chance to deal with what's being read out. Mr. Baqaj, we've got this statement in front of us, and you've heard the bits that have been read out so far. Is there anything you want to say about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say this. But those who took me in for questioning in Peja wrote what they wanted. This list of names has been shown to me by the man who took me into questioning, and I merely saw it in Peja.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of the statement, since we don't have a lot of time I have to skip a lot, you say: "I note that I am in contact with Aljaj Hakija, a cook in the staff, and in contacts with him I found out that for the needs of the DTGs in Kosovo and Metohija weapons are being brought by both from Germany and Switzerland to the port of Vlora, Republic of Albania, and then by lorry to Tropoje." And then at the end, it says: "The citizen has read the record and hereby signs it." And there is your signature here as well as the signature of the authorised officials to whom you provided the statement. Is this your statement, Mr. Baqaj?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: It is my signature but it's not my statement. I don't know this person whom you mentioned, and I have no idea who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that you have no idea about anything that you talked about before, but by the way, can you tell me, since a little while ago in response to Mr. Ryneveld's questions, you said that one of those killed next to you to the Dubrava prison was Ramiz Memija from Tropoje. So he was a citizen of the Republic of Albania. Why was he arrested? Was he arrested as a member of the KLA or not? He was arrested on the territory of the Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know why he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This caravan that you met with weapons, do you know what kind of weapons were being transported in the caravan?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I said I didn't see any convoy with weapons coming into Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I read your statement, and it states there that it was a convoy of 200 horses and 200 members of the KLA with weapons, and now you claim that you didn't say that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I didn't say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Who was responsible in the -- in Kosovo on behalf of the government in Tropoje for distributing those weapons? The so-called government of Kosovo in Tropoje?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that either. Very well. You said that you met Tahir Zemaj in the Tri Brata cafe. Was he a member of the KLA as well? Just answer yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know where this cafe is nor do I know Tahir Zemaj. I know him as a name but I don't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is also not true that you met him there. Is this also something that was made up by the team of investigators who talked to you, that you had met Tahir Zemaj in the Three Brothers, Tri Brata cafe? You didn't say that either, did you?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I didn't say this, and I say again that I don't know Tahir Zemaj and I've never had contact are him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you read a book with the interviews of Tahir Zemaj and Ramush Haradinaj? Did you read that, at least? This was published. Anyone can buy that in Kosovo, I assume.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No, I've never read it. I've heard about it. But personally, I have not read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement to The Hague investigators, you said that before the military authorities you denied being a member of the KLA. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I have denied this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And you say that they showed you a list that contained 74 names of Albanians who had been smuggling weapons from Albania. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: That's true. They showed me this list in Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there was a warrant out for all of your arrests?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that on the 6th of September, at 7.00 a.m., you were taken to the police station in Djakovica. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9261 to 9269.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you were questioned by the investigators and inspectors. One of them was called Zita, as well as the Pec security chief, Dem Mujaj, who you say you knew very well from before the war. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how you knew the chief of security in Pec, Dem Mujaj?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I only knew him as a face.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You knew him only by sight. But you said you knew him very well before the war, in the statement that you provided for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I knew him by sight, but I had never talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps an associate of the state security after you got acquainted with Dem Mujaj perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he was not acquainted with Mr. Mujaj. He simply knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will skip questions relating to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So during your questioning before the head of state security Mujaj and a police officer named Zita, subsequently admitted that you were a member of the KLA. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I did admit this. And anybody in my position would have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you detained until the trial when you were sentenced to 18 months by a court in Pec?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that no one mistreated you when you were in prison?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I wasn't mistreated in Peja prison because some of the prison guards were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that it wasn't just some of them. Could you please tell me whether at least one-half of the guards in the Pec prison were Albanians? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I think it was half of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us now move to the Dubrava prison. On the 21st of December, you were transferred there, and you were put into block C, with prisoners who had not yet been sentenced. They were all wearing civilian clothes, just like in any investigative prison before they were convicted. Only convicted convicts wear prison uniforms. Was that clear?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You started to serve your sentence in February 1999 in Dubrava. From the point when you started serving your sentence until the bombardment while you were serving in Dubrava prison, did anybody mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many Albanian guards worked in the prison?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: There was not a single Albanian in Dubrava prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Nexhmedin Kalicinaj [phoen] the deputy warden of the Dubrava prison?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was killed in the bombing. Do you know that not a single Albania, or not a single inmate, neither a Serb or an Albanian, was brought to that prison without being brought for trial proceedings before that? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I didn't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You met the other inmates in the prison. Did you meet a single prisoner who was arrested and had not been brought before a court for trial proceedings?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: While I was there, everybody in my cell had been unconvicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were not convicted. They were not charged. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I said they had not been convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were under criminal investigation. The proceedings, the criminal investigation proceedings were under way. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the C1 block, which was hit right away, was a block that was under stricter supervision?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the most dangerous criminals were placed in that block?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of criminals there were. I don't know what you're driving at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me, was the security command post hit at that time in that pavilion?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: The C1 block was hit twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it true to say that, in the first strike, the security services building was targeted?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I know that there were three shots. Which one was first, I don't know, because we were inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that there's any connection between the targeting of the security services building and the hitting of the wall with bombs?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I said I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the picture showing the destruction of the periphery wall or perimeter wall of the prison. But we won't wait. I'll continue with my cross-examination, so please show it to the witness when you trace it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The exhibits produced by the accused, the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
