utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many workers of the security service were wounded during the first strike?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know that. We were inside the walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you when the attack ended?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Which attack are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When that first attack was over, where were you?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I was housed in C2 block.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the picture of the wall that had been destroyed. Yes, that one. Please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the destroyed wall of the prison. A moment ago, Mr. Ryneveld asked you whether a truck could pass and you said it couldn't. Don't you think, seeing the picture now, that a truck could pass through this hole in the wall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, in fairness to the witness, there has been an identification of this wall. Just help us with this, Mr. Baqaj; do you recognise the wall, first of all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I recognise this wall very well. This is not where we prisoners were. This was on the left-hand side. Here there was the central heating plant for the prison, and this was outside the wall where the other buildings were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you link the hitting of the wall with the hitting of the building with the guards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's nothing to do with him. You'll have to ask those who targeted the prison. He can't deal with that. Have you finished with the photograph now, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you finished -- have you finished with the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let it come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that additional security measures were introduced to prevent the prisoners from escaping?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the aim of those measures was to protect the prisoners from possible settling of accounts amongst themselves?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No. It was no doubt in order to exterminate us all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me now, Mr. Baqaj, how do you explain that someone intends to exterminate you all and then after that, as you yourself say in this statement, using 15 buses, according to data I have, more than 800 of you were transported to other prisons, and those who had served their sentence were released home on time, et cetera. How do you explain that somebody had the intention of exterminating you and then transported 800 of you to safety?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: We had seen what had happened inside. And about 160 prisoners were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that 93 killed prisoners, that their bodies were pulled out of the rubble and that this number that you mention of 160, you're really referring to the number of injured, not the number of dead. Isn't that right, Mr. Baqaj?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: The number of those injured was larger, and there were 160 killed, or 180 including the 23 killed by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know exactly how many were killed in the NATO bombing, and you're reducing it to the number of 23, and you're claiming that the rest were killed by prison guards. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I saw these 23 people myself with my own eyes and I counted them, each of them. These were the people killed by the NATO attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In all the days of the NATO strikes -- well, how many days was the prison bombed?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: The prison was bombed on the 19th of May, the 21st of May, and then there were no more NATO bombings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, then, how probable is what you're claiming on page 7 of your statement? "While we were in Lipjan, the guards ordered the prisoners from Dubrava not to say anything about what had happened in Dubrava. If we were ever asked, we were to say that all the prisoners were killed by NATO." Is it probable that 800 of you were persuaded by the guards and that these guards, who wanted to exterminate you, would believe you that you would do them the service of saying that NATO had killed them? Who could accept such an assumption?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all a matter of argument. This is all argument, Mr. Milosevic, as you know. Now, if you've got a question, you can ask it, but that's not a proper one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I do have questions. You have fixed my time, and I will use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you were finally evacuated and after transferred, as far as I gather, to Sremska Mitrovica, or where was it you ended up? Yes. You were released on the 6th of March, 2000 from Sremska Mitrovica. How many time did you spend in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I spent about nine months in the prison at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it occur to you that in those nine months spent in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica - so you were far from Kosovo, you were in a regular prison in the north of Serbia - did it occur to you to inform one of the authorities, the warden or his assistant or anyone, of the fact that the prison guards wanted to kill you and that they actually killed some of your colleagues in prison? Did it occur to you to report this to anyone, to report what had happened to you to anyone?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many more of you from Dubrava were housed in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know about the other cells, but in mine there were 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nine from Dubrava? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I said there were 90 brought from Dubrava in my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this translation is correct. Is there a cell in prison that can take 90 men?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: The room was about 20 metres long, and there were 90 people sitting on the floor. It was about 20 metres by six.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't have a bed in Sremska Mitrovica during those nine months you spent there?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Not a single prisoner in Sremska Mitrovica had a bed. We were all on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I must say that I hear that for the first time, but I can't question you any further about that. It sounds too improbable to me. Tell me, please, at the time of the bombing of the prison in Dubrava, did anyone escape or try to escape?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard that certain persons tried to escape, but they did not succeed. That day that we were transferred to the prison in Lipjan, I saw the bodies at the entrance of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone try to persuade you, among the more dangerous criminals, shall we call them that, to try to escape?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Me personally? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that during the NATO attacks on the prison, crews of domestic and foreign reporters would come, take photographs and film and prepare reports about the bombing of the prison? Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No? Very well. Is it true that a team, together with the investigating judge, came to carry out an on-site inspection?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes. On 20th of May, they came. I saw a cameraman there, and certain persons of Roma nationality came with a tractor to pick up the three bodies that were killed -- of persons who were killed on 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as you know, was that investigation suspended because of the bombing, in which the investigating judge was wounded, but the investigation continued for several days in succession? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I was in my cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that this large bombing raid caused panic, great panic, among the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: There was panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you hid in those manholes and drains, and when they forced you to come out, did they throw teargas inside to force you out?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: On the morning of 22nd of May, at 6.00 in the morning, I was in the manhole and they called me and said we should line up on the sports hall and that we would be transferred to the prison in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. After this event that you describe that they shot at you but didn't kill you and then you went to the gymnasium and then you said the guards then brought you cigarettes sent by the commander of the prison, food and so on. So they wanted to kill you for a while, and then they gave you cigarettes and food. And then after that, the next day or the day after, it doesn't matter after all, they put you into those 15 buses and drive you off to another prison. Is that your whole story?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: On the 23rd of May, that is to say I spent the night of the 22nd of May in the basement of the kitchen. In the morning, at about 5.00, police forces entered, guards as well. They were firing in manholes where prisoners were hiding. They threw hand grenades and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they throwing teargas or bombs or grenades?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I said that in those manholes where prisoners were hiding, they were throwing bombs, hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in the manhole?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't have interpretation. I said that on the night of the 21st of May, I was in the manhole until 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone throw a hand grenade at you?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: That night, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone throw a hand grenade at you in the manhole that other night? Or day, it doesn't matter when. Did anyone throw a hand grenade at you?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: The night when the hand grenades were thrown, I said I was in the kitchen basement, but I said I saw people inside the manholes who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned to you the 93 bodies pulled out of the rubble. Do you know that each of those bodies has been identified, that the complete crime processing, photographs were taken, and that all this was done by a doctor, a surgeon from the hospital in Pec, and that there are complete records about this that I have been able to see. Nowhere is there any mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you don't know this, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know where these rubbles that he's mentioning were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have one minute more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, if it's just one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While serving your sentence in Sremska Mitrovica, did you have any problems whatsoever, and did any one of the Albanians have any problems in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: When I served my sentence, I was escorted by the International Red Cross Committee to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you who escorted you after you had completed serving your sentence. When you were released, you were released exactly on the day when your sentence had been completed. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I can't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. To save time, I'm not asking you what happened after you served your sentence but during the time you were in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica, the nine and a half months spent there. Did you or any one of the other Albanians imprisoned in Sremska Mitrovica have any kind of problems? Did anyone mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes. There were lots of problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of problems?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: There was beating. Hygiene conditions were poor, food as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming that in the prison that was under the competence of the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Serbia where you were serving your sentence, that you were beaten up, as were the other Albanians. Is that what you're saying? In the prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I was personally beaten as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who beat you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who beat you, Mr. Baqaj? Who? Please give me the name. You met all those people during the nine and a half months you spent there; who beat you?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: The prison guards. I don't know their names. I don't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to deal with matters which are at the LiveNote transcript, page 30, line 1, and within the statement at page 7, line 10 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You gave evidence today concerning a list of names of people you say were killed in the sports field by the camp guards. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your statement that you made to the Tribunal, you told them that you didn't know -- you could not remember the names of people who were killed at the prison.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I knew some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your statement, you said, "I knew some of them, but now I cannot remember their names.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I mentioned some names, some that came on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your statement -- in your evidence today, you gave a list of names, including one Memija Ramiz. Do you remember that name?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you said that he was one killed close by in the sports field.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Ramiz Memija was killed as well near the sports field but by a sniper that fired from the watchtower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. In your statement, I'm looking at page 6, in the middle: "During the day, snipers fired from the watchtowers and I remember that one prisoner, Memija Ramiz from Tropoje in Albania was shot and killed by a sniper." The other names that you gave today, Hamdija Demaj, Izet Beqiraj, Fadil Beqiri, how did you remember those names?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I remembered those names because they were close by, close to my location. And the next day -- and I also remember them from the next day when we went to count the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm also looking at the prosecutor's summary, paragraph 15, page 3. Have you been referring to any notes while you've been giving evidence about those names?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What piece of paper do you have?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have those names written on a piece of paper, that you gave today?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you look at that while you were giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who wrote that paper or wrote those names on the paper?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I wrote those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you write those names on the paper?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: When I was in Kosovo, in my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Two months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And why did you write those names on the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Because I remembered that these persons who were killed that day on the sports field were close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, but could I make the observation that if witnesses are referring to lists or names on pieces of paper, it's desirable that the Trial Chamber or the OTP should know about it so that one can see what sources they're using whilst they're giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Baqaj -- Mr. Baqaj, are you hearing me?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One of the matters we have to consider is the demeanour of a witness, that is, how the witness appears to us, and I have to say that I have been struck by just how sad, how melancholy and withdrawn you appear. Can you tell me whether you have been like that all your life or is this something relatively new?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: I've been like this throughout my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Are you suffering, as far as you're aware, then, from any effects of the experience that you had?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Three ribs on the right-hand side have been broken in the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. And are they now broken or have you received treatment for that?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Partly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you now working?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No, I'm not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And have you been -- have you worked at all since the -- since the conflict?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Baqaj, I'd like to ask some questions about the events which happened in Dubrava prison. When you were lined up early in the morning, the 22nd, and even after the shooting took place, were there any prisoners who tried to escape out of the prison at that time?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it's about the people who were killed in the manhole: Was it that they tried to escape through the manhole or they're just hiding inside the manhole?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: They were hiding in manholes, trying to find a more secure place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit 289, which is the aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a photograph by Mr. Milosevic about a large hole in what you say you recalled as being an area that you knew. I'm not going to show you that photograph, but I'm going to ask you to look --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Oh, do you have the colour version? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript should say this is Mr. Ryneveld instead of Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not looking at the transcript. Thank you for catching that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir -- could we show that on the -- do you see the photograph there, sir? Can you tell us, in relation to this larger aerial view, where in relation to the wall, if it is depicted in this photograph, where that hole in the wall is? Are you -- do you know? Perhaps we can orient --

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: It's a little bit further from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps I can ask you these questions: Do you see that the wall on the left-hand -- the left-hand side seems to extend beyond where it says -- I can't read it now --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There's an administration building and then the square below that. What does that say? "Front gate."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you see where the front gate is on that photograph, near the administration building?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That appears to be an intersection of a wall that runs horizontally across the photograph and a wall that runs sort of vertically, continuing in a northerly direction. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did that wall continue beyond the perimeter of the prison itself?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Outside the buildings, there was another wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This hole in the wall shown to you by the accused, did you see that hole in the wall while you were a prisoner during the month of May, 1999, in the prison?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: After the bombing, I was in my cell on the second floor, and I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And where did you see that hole? Can you -- is the location of that hole shown in this photograph, Exhibit 289?

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: It's very far. I cannot tell. But I said it was on the left side of the block where I was housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And can you find that for us? If you can't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Here. This is -- this was the wall of the prison, and this was a separate wall that went further down the line, and here is the part where the wall was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can you point to the place where the wall was destroyed, if you see it? I'm sorry. If you did, it didn't show up on the ELMO. You're now pointing in the area beyond the prison proper; is that correct? This is the exterior perimeter wall.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GANI BAQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's right that the statement which was put to the witness in cross-examination by the accused, the record of the interview in Pec, should be exhibited and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those statements will be -- the B/C/S and the English will be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 301.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Possibly a Defence exhibit number, since they were produced by him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. Scratch that. It will be Defence Exhibit 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Baqaj, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have another witness, Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, she's here and ready to go, but I'd say we're six minutes away from the normal adjourning time; do you want me to start or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We will take the adjournment now. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Sofije Imeraj. And this witness, Your Honours, deals with issues about Padaliste, and you've heard from another lady a couple days ago by the same surname, Imeraj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Ms. Imeraj, I understand correctly you are 21 years old, you're currently unmarried, and you are a Kosovo Albanian young woman from the town of Padaliste in the municipality of Istok; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And on the 26th of March, 1999, were you living in your home with your parents, Hasan and Hyra, and your two brothers, Muhamet and Jeton, in Padaliste?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you give a statement to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 25th of November, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And on the 6th of March of this year, 2002, were you given an opportunity to review that statement in your language, in Albanian, and have an opportunity to make whatever corrections that needed to be made, and then were you asked by a presiding officer of this Tribunal whether that statement was true and accurate to the best of your recollection and belief?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that statement be marked at this time, Your Honours, as an exhibit. And this time I will wait for the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 301.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. While it's being distributed, Your Honours, I would propose to read a summary of what is contained in that statement for highlights. Your Honours, according to this witness's statement, which you are about to receive, she tells about an incident on the 26th of March, 1999, when Serb forces and tanks surrounded Padaliste the previous day, the 25th of March, and prevented villagers from leaving. Avdyl Imeraj, the witness's father's uncle, and his family - five people in total - arrived at their place in order to seek shelter and safety. Apparently all were concerned and worried about what the Serb forces might do, because they'd heard that Serb officials had said that if NATO bombed, Albanians in Kosovo would suffer. Well, the next morning, the 26th of March, 1999, the witness describes in her statement how between 6.00 a.m. and 6.30 a.m. of that morning, they were all preparing to leave Padaliste when the village was attacked by Serb soldiers on foot. She describes how three soldiers dressed in green camouflage uniforms came to her house. One smashed the front window and fired his automatic rifle into the room. Apparently her father said to this soldier, "Don't do that, Neighbour." The soldier replied, "There are no more neighbours." One of the soldiers then entered the house and the third soldier remained in the courtyard. Her father, brother Muhamet, and uncle Avdyl were ordered out of the house. Her mother pleaded with them to leave Muhamet, her first son after the birth of four daughters, but to no avail. When he was also taken out, her mother then fainted. As her father, brother, and uncle left the house, she saw the soldier at the window kneel down and fire his automatic rifle at the men continuously for several seconds. One of the women who understood Serbian heard one of the soldiers say, "Leave the other ones here. We'll come back later and catch them and burn them." When the soldiers had left, the women went out and found the bodies of the men lying immediately outside the front door. The witness describes in her statement the soldier at the window who shot her father, brother, and uncle, and she says she heard him being called "Pero," which she believes is short for the Serbian first name of Predrag. When they checked on their neighbour's home, they found that Beka Imeraj and eight members of his family had also been killed. The witness and the other occupants remained in the house until about 11.30 a.m., when they decided to leave. They made their way to local woods where they sheltered the rest of that day, until about 10.00 p.m. Then they left for Uq, a village in the mountains, where they spent the night. Well, Uq village came under shell attack early the next morning, and the witness and her family and others were forced yet again to flee. They went to the woods at the mountain known as Fushe e Madhe. They remained there with thousands of others from various villages for two weeks before walking to Rozaje in Montenegro. That journey took two nights and three days. She and her family eventually made it to Albania where they remained until the end of the war. When returning to their home in Padaliste at the end of August, they noted that their house had been badly damaged and looted, with everything stolen. The windows were broken, there were bullet holes everywhere, and the three cows were missing. They found the bodies of her father, brother, and uncle Avdyl buried close to the well in their garden. That is a very basic summary of some of the highlights contained in this witness's statement, and I have no additional questions to ask her. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I start with the cross-examination, I would like to ask Mr. Ryneveld to be kind enough to give me a piece of information. As an interpreter, on the first page here of the witness's statement, the name is stated Besnik Sokoli. Is that the Sokoli who already testified here in the course of the past six or seven months?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Insofar as is relevant, you can ask the Court. Mr. Ryneveld, can you help as to that or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm having some difficulty locating the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The reference is on the first page. The interpreter is described as Mr. Sokoli, and it's said that a witness of that name, as indeed my recollection also, gave evidence. Yes, he was the eighth witness. Do you know whether he's the same man or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I don't want to indicate without checking. Perhaps I can provide that information later. It may be the same name. Of course, many names are similar and I wouldn't want to hazard a guess without giving a correct answer. So I'll check that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems to be the number eight witness who gave evidence on the 22nd of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Although I need to check it out, our case manager, who knows these things, is nodding in agreement that it is the same person. So unless I tell you otherwise, my understanding is that it is in fact the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It's just been confirmed, apparently. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that he is an employee of this institution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with this witness. She's here to give evidence. Cross-examine her and then you can raise these other matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you live in Padaliste the entire time, and you were born there as well?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the activities of the KLA in your region in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: No. In my region, there was no KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody from your family or any one of your relatives belong to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: No, no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that there was another family in your house, the family of your father's uncle. And Mr. Ryneveld also stated this a little while ago. And the family arrived the day before because it would be safer there. Where did that family come from?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: The family wasn't there two days earlier, but they came in the night when the Serb forces surrounded the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood from your statement that your father's uncle lived close by. Did he live close to you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. He lived near, close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How close?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How close?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: He lived about 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was the sense of him not feeling safe in his own house and feeling safer in your house which was only 50 metres further away? What is the sense of that if the difference is only 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: He came to us because your forces, your Chetniks, were near his house on the hill in Padalishte, above the hill, above the village. They were -- his house was at the end, near the hill, and our house was more near the valley, on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which Chetniks are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Your -- the thugs that work for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the police officers or the soldiers or the police and the soldiers? Who are you thinking of when you say that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I mean your police and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So he felt threatened because they were close to his house, and your house is 50 metres away from his house, so -- and that is why he felt safer. That's why he came to your house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat that. That was her evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did your uncle's father have any reason to hide?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Your father's uncle," interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't come to us to hide. Your forces were shooting, and he came in our direction, towards the valley, to get away from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you find out from him that the police entered your village?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I didn't find out from him. The police had a checkpoint, a point of control on the hill just over the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it had that checkpoint for a long time. It wasn't there just from that day.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They had been there for quite awhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you knew that NATO had started bombing. My question is as follows: What did you personally see of this bombing?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat that? Which bombing are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: You said that you knew that NATO had started its bombing. You knew about it. So I'm asking you what did you personally see of this bombing? What was it that you knew from personal experience?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see anything. I just knew that NATO had bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And another quote from your statement about how somebody, allegedly from the Serbian government, stated that when NATO started its bombing, then the Albanians in Kosovo would suffer. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point is, it says in your statement: "I heard someone -- that someone in the Serbian government had said that if NATO bombed, then the Albanians in Kosovo would suffer." Did you in fact hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before you tell me who it was who stated this on television, could you please tell me if Kosovo was bombed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there's no dispute about that. What she said is that she saw nothing of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But is it -- is it disputed that the majority of the population in Kosovo are Albanians? Is this disputed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Just ask the witness some relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If somebody bombs the territory populated by a majority of Albanians, wouldn't these Albanians be the ones who would suffer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just ask the witness what she saw or who it was who said it, what programme it was on. You can ask questions of that sort, but there's no point arguing with her.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I am asking her, Mr. May, who was it who said this. Was this somebody threatening the Albanians, somebody from the Serbian government threatening that the Albanians would suffer if NATO were to bomb?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You say you heard this on television. Can you tell us who it was who said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the television, on the news from Belgrade one, Television One, and they said it in Serb. It was the forces of Milosevic which said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste time with this. Obviously you don't know who said this. Well, nobody could have said that as a threat, but let us continue. Were you frightened when you found out that NATO had started its bombing?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I wasn't afraid of NATO, I was afraid of your forces, because NATO didn't come to kill us, it came to save us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When NATO bombed Kosovo, weren't you afraid of those bombs? Do you think that bombs differentiate between the ethnic groups and that they would only kill Serbs and not kill Albanians? Is that the reason why you were not afraid?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, would you put the question in its proper form then? This girl says that she wasn't afraid of the bombs, she was afraid of Serbs. Well, of course I expected her to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's her answer. So there's no point arguing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were not afraid of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear how many Albanians in different cases -- for example, scores of Albanians were killed in certain incidents by NATO planes. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any Albanian was killed by the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I said I didn't know, and I don't think any Albanians were killed by NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is the feeling in Kosovo right now, that nobody was killed by NATO. In your statement, you say that you woke up, that you were drinking coffee, that you were getting dressed, and that you were getting ready to flee. Doesn't it seem to you that this is pretty cold-blooded and quite casual, if you wish to flee; getting up, drinking coffee, and getting ready to flee? Does it seem as if you were in mortal danger in that case?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: We got up in the morning. Some were having coffee and some weren't. We didn't want to leave right away from our house, but when your forces came and surrounded the village, then we had to get away because we were afraid of your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said that you tried to escape the night before but that you were returned, turned back. Who was it that turned you back?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I didn't say the night before we didn't want to go. I said that my uncle came the night before to our house. I didn't say that we wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you decide to leave the house, since he arrived the night before and informed you that the village was surrounded? When did you finally decide to escape?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: My uncle came the night earlier and spent the night at our place. But when your forces arrived right in front of the door, then we left immediately; we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did our forces do if they were there up until the morning? What were they doing during the night?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Your forces came in the morning, at 6.30 in the morning that they appeared. And what they were doing, you would know better than I. You've got my statement in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understood that you said that they had surrounded you already the previous night. But let's not waste time on that. Had they surrounded you the previous night or are you still claiming that they came in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Serb forces arrived in the evening and went in the direction of Mitrovica. They stayed a few minutes on the street, on the road, they shot a couple of times, and then went on, carried on immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the uncle saw soldiers in the morning. How far away were they?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: My uncle saw the soldiers surrounding the village. When he saw them, that they'd surrounded the whole village, he came in to our place and told us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you see them as well?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: They were coming towards the houses to kill and massacre Albanians who had done nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you saw them approaching the houses; is that right? You said that your father told your brother Muhamet to hide in the neighbour's basement. Do you have another brother?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I have another brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did he say that to Muhamet only? Why didn't he say the same thing to the other brother? Where was he?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Because the other brother was small, whereas Muhamet was older.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that three soldiers came to your house. When you refer to your house in your statement, do you also imply the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: There was one soldier at the window, one came in, and one stayed outside, around the house, looking around the house, behind the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where was the third one?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: One was at the window, one was in the courtyard, looking around to see that no one was coming, and the third one was inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you say the soldier broke the glass of the with his rifle. Did you see that? With the --

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that he pointed the gun through the window and fired in the direction of your mother and brother; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, Mr. Ryneveld said that he opened a burst of fire. Did he fire a single shot or a burst of fire in the direction of your mother and your brother?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: He shot one time, to kill my brother Muhamet who was sitting by my mother. My mother intervened and protected my brother, and the bullet passed by and entered the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was shooting at your brother - you're sure of that - through the window into the room. So he was only a couple of metres away from them. And then, thanks to what your mother did, he missed him; is that right? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm loath to interject, but it's been suggested that I put in the summary something that wasn't put in the summary. When I talked about the burst of fire, I indicated it was at the men. I did not talk about the shooting incident at the women. And the summary speaks for itself, but he's left that suggestion, and I thought it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic, you're asking the witness to repeat something which she's already said, so move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did I understand you correctly that your father addressed this soldier who broke your window with the word "Neighbour"? Did he know him? Are you claiming that this was indeed your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. My father -- when the window was broke, he said, "You're our neighbour." He said, "Don't do this. We are neighbours." And he replied, "We have been neighbours up until today. We are not neighbours any more." And my father recognised this soldier, and I recognised this soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the name of that soldier?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Predrag Belosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you're saying now doesn't sound convincing if you inferred, and you say in your statement, that someone addressed someone with the word "Pero," with the name "Pero," and on the basis of that, you drew the conclusion that his name was Predrag; is that right? Because you heard somebody call somebody "Pero," you inferred that his name was Predrag. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I heard the soldier calling the name of Pero, but my father said, "Don't be afraid, don't get scared, because it's him, our neighbour Predrag."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the short name for Predrag most often is not Pero? "Pero" is the short name for Petar and not for Predrag.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: That was his name. And his real name was Predrag Belosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what it says in your statement, I will ask you something now, and answer me. I believe that you drew this conclusion from somebody's explanation rather than on the basis of your own knowledge. This is what it says at the end of your statement: "The soldier who was in the yard called out to the soldier with the word 'Pero.'" And then in the next sentence, it says: "'Pero' is a nickname for someone who is named Predrag." "Pero" is the abbreviation for somebody who is called Petar and not Predrag. And then you go on to say: "I have been told that there was a policeman at the police checkpoint located at the stop of Rakosh hill who was called Predrag Belosevic and that he comes from Cerkolez." So you're claiming in this statement that you were told that at the checkpoint there was a policeman called Predrag Belosevic. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I recognised the soldier very well because he was our neighbour. I knew he was from Cerkolez, and I knew he was Predrag, while those who called him Pero were your thugs. And they called him Pero. Personally, I recognised him as Predrag and my father recognised him as Predrag, and he comes from Cerkolez and he is today in Cerkolez now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you know him so well, how is it possible that in your statement you said, "I have been told that there was a policeman at the police checkpoint at the top of Rakosh hill who was called Predrag Belosevic"? If what you say is true, wouldn't you have said, "I knew the policeman called so and so," instead of saying, "I have been told that there was policeman called Predrag Belosevic," that somebody told you that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: It's a mistake, because nobody told me anything. These are my words. I said that I recognised him, that I've seen him at the checkpoint in Rakosh, and that I've seen him there several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I was just quoting from your written statement, therefore, I had the impression that somebody had told you of Belosevic in order to charge him. That appeared to me to be obvious. Now you're claiming something else and that you didn't say what it says here. But let us move on. And this soldier who broke the window and then fired a shot in the direction of your mother and brother could have simply entered the house if his intention was to kill somebody in that house. Why would he shoot through the window?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: He broke the window, and he fired a shot at my brother Muhamet in order to kill him in the lap of my mother Hyra so that my mother could see her dead son in her own lap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For heaven's sake. You think it's a sadist who wanted to kill the son in front of his mother?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The witness can't say why the solder did what he did. All she can say is what happened, and she's described that. She can't give a motive for this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, she's just mentioning those motives, which seem to me rather extreme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone take care of your mother when she fainted?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: There was no one to look after her except me. Do you think that your forces would have looked after her? Their intention was to kill us, not to look after us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any one of you take care of your mother when she fainted? Who did? Who cared for her?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I did. I got up immediately, and I brought her a glass of water, and I was trying to bring her back to consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you saw the soldier shooting next to the window. Did you see only him shooting or within your field of vision was also your brother, father, uncle, and all the others? Did you see him only as he fired that shot into the house or did you see him firing in some other direction as well? What exactly did you see through the window?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I saw when the soldier approached the window and said to my father and my father's uncle and my brother to come outside. When they took them outside, I saw the soldier very well as he kneeled down and as he fired in their direction. I saw this with my own eyes. I saw him killing them with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me, please, did you see any kind of shooting, apart from the one that you've just described, that you saw a soldier kneeling and firing in the direction of your family? At that point in time, you didn't see your family members, only the soldier shooting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I saw how he lined them up against the threshold, and I saw very well how the soldier kneeled down and how he fired in their direction, and I saw when the three of them actually fell down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that: "When Muhamet, my father, and uncle went outside, I saw that soldier from the window kneel down and without a word start shooting. It was rapid and continuous shooting of several seconds. I didn't hear anyone utter a sound until those soldiers left." And so on. You heard them having this conversation. "Leave the rest there. We'll catch them later," and so on. So you're claiming that actually that soldier executed the members of your family and you saw that with your own eyes.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I saw it with my own eyes, and I heard it perfectly well when he said, "Leave them there. We will come back again and we will burn them."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when this was happening, the event that you have described, was there any other shooting in the vicinity in your village? Could anything else be heard except what you describe that allegedly took place in your house?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I did not hear -- I heard that the village was surrounded from all sides by your forces, and they were shooting, firing in the direction of our house. Their intention was to burn the house. When those soldiers left, my sister-in-law got up and she went to turn off the electricity because she thought that there might be fire because there was firing in the direction of the house at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that only your house in the village was attacked or was there a lot of other shooting around you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: There was a lot of shooting around us. And the entire village -- for example, 19 members of the Imeraj family were killed by your forces, and six were buried. There were shooting, firing, and massacres throughout the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you claiming that there was no fighting there or was there fighting between the police and some KLA forces? Was there any combat there or was there none?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: I didn't say there were KLA forces. In the beginning, I mentioned that there was no KLA in our region, in the village of Padalishte, in the Imeraj neighbourhood. There was no KLA. But it was the firing of your forces, their killings, their massacres. There was no KLA there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not asking you whether the KLA from your village was engaged in fighting with the police in your village. I'm just asking in general terms about the KLA whose unit could have come from some other village or some other area and engaged in combat with the army and the police right there or in the immediate vicinity of your houses. Could that perhaps have been the case or not? Was there any kind of conflict going on at the time?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: No. Between the KLA and your forces, no. There were only your forces killing the village, the Imeraj family. There was no KLA in the Imeraj neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, what was the exact date when this happened?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in the house after this alleged killing?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: We stayed there until about 11.00 a.m., 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that after that you went to the woods. Did you go to the woods alone?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: The whole family left the house. On our left side we saw my father, uncle, and brother killed. We proceeded -- we proceeded towards the courtyard of Beka Imeraj's house, who was killed together with seven other members of his family, and then we proceeded in the direction of Cerkolez, but there was no place for us to go because the whole neighbourhood was also surrounded, and the only possibility left was for us to take to the woods. And throughout the way, I saw dead bodies. I saw buried bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw buried bodies? When did you see those buried bodies?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Not buried, but they had bullet wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And how far was Tahir Imeraj's house from the woods?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: It wasn't far away. Maybe 300 to 400 metres, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, how far is the mountain you went to from the village?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: When we were fleeing towards the mountain, we changed our position two to three times, because your forces who committed the killing in the Imeraj neighbourhood, they would come again to the mountains and ask for men in order to kill them. They killed everything they saw in front of them; women, children, elderly, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you went in a tractor to the woods, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: That night we walked. We went on foot. We didn't go by tractor because we couldn't go by tractor. All the tractors and all other vehicles were destroyed. We went through the maintain. We passed the Cerkolez-Padalishte road. And as soon as we crossed the road, your forces again came and we sought shelter in the mountain, and we went then to the village of Uq. And Ali Tahiri, whose house is in this village, we spent the night in his house. The following morning, we woke up and the whole village had already fled to the mountain. And then we set off. My mother Hyra could not walk. She was not able to walk. And we placed my mother in a tractor while the rest of us, we proceeded on foot to the mountains, to the place called Fushe e Madhe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So what I was asking you about the tractor means that only your mother was on the tractor up to Velika Poljane, because she couldn't walk, and the rest of you were on foot. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: My mother got on the tractor, on the tractor which belonged to the house where we were staying in Uq, and we took things to take with us to the mountains, but we couldn't all get on, so we put on the tractor my mother, who couldn't walk, and we ourselves, we walked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But from that place, as far as I can understand from your statement, you walked towards Rozaje. So you crossed over into Montenegro and went to Rozaje. And you walked for two nights and three days. Is that so or isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was your mother with you at the time? Did she walk with you for two nights and three days?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: My mother couldn't walk fast but slowly, rather late, supporting her -- there was my brother Jeton and I supporting her. We managed to complete the journey in two nights and three days. And then we finally made it to Rozaje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: We went to Albania by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From Rozaje.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJE IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, from Rozaje to Albania by bus.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nothing arising. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Imeraj, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for inviting me to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know who is next. Mr. Saxon, I think since it's Friday, we might as well call it a day. It's ten minutes before we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next witness, Your Honour, will be Behar Haxhiavdija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll hear him on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. I think Mr. Ryneveld might have a point right now to raise with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours. K13's statement is now available, and we'll ask that that be provided. And secondly, in response to the question that I said I would check out about Mr. Sokoli --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we -- let's deal with one thing at a time. Let's deal with K13.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. We have copies of K13's 92 bis package, and we would ask that be marked as an exhibit in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld. What was your other point?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Fine. We will await a number in a moment. I suspect it will be 302 or something. But the other thing was just the question that was posed to me through the Court about Mr. Sokoli, the eighth witness. My understanding is that he in fact was employed by the OTP for a period of time but not when he gave evidence. He was not an employee of the OTP when he gave his evidence. He acted as a translator for some witness statements in an intervening period. And the evidence he gave before this Court was about a time period before he ever became an employee as an interpreter. So, yes, it is the same man; yes, he was employed by the OTP for a period of time but not concerning the time period when he testified about what had occurred nor at the time he gave evidence itself. That's the best answer I can give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The original of K13's statement will be marked as 302, under seal. The first redacted version will be 302A. The public redacted version will be 302B. 302A will also be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Nine o'clock Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of September, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
